278.s: He hears reggae in early Fats Domino.

803.s: He says Australian music is derivative, then explains the meaning of 'Waltzing Matilda'.
803.q: That’s interesting because Australia, culturally speaking, doesn’t really have an identity. And I think it’s kind of fascinating. It’s something you don’t realize until you’re out of it, but Australia’s music, Australia’s cuisine, Australia’s culture, it’s old, based on something else. So if we…

340.t: Is jazz America's only original art form?
340.s: Rowe raises the cliche about jazz being America's only art form and asks about blues, rock and bluegrass.

64.t: Oral culture versus written history of jazz
64.s: Asked about oral versus literate culture, Taylor links jazz to the griot tradition, the banning of drums, and first-person interviews.
64.q: Jazz coming from an African-American point of view, having been created by Africans and their subsequent generations, has continued the same tradition, the griot, and since Africans and African-American slaves were, it was against the law to teach them to read and write in many states, they had to…

702.t: Life lessons, Hugh Masekela and the African rhythms behind jazz
702.s: He says to put the music first, tells how Masekela corrected his cha-cha as a Mozambican rhythm, and traces how African music evolved differently across the Americas.
702.q: Well it’s all connected. It’s all connected. If you’ve going to really play this music you’ve got to live the music. And you always put the music first. People that are entertainers — well a musician is an entertainer of sorts — but there’s a deeper quality to it as well. It’s not just the comedian…

220.t: Jazz as black folk music, not just improvisation
220.s: Asked about jazz education, Wess argues jazz is a black folk music and a way of life, not merely improvisation.
220.q: Well, you’ve got quite a few good players and then you’ve got some that they’re not really in tune with the music. You see, people get the idea that jazz is improvisation, but it’s a lot more than that. Actually, jazz is folk music. It’s one of the many forms of black folk music. You got a whole…

565.t: Rumba, African roots and the word salsa
565.s: He explains rumba's origins among African captives, its derivatives, and why he calls lumping them together as salsa a misnomer.
565.ch: Latin music history and the Palladium
565.q: Well, that’s the African captives. They were captives. They turned you into a slave, but you were a captive. They took you away from where you were born by force. So when they arrived, particularly in Cuba... They were distributed all over the Caribbean, but mostly in Cuba, no? First they took the…

583.t: Jazz as a response to slavery and the search for freedom
583.s: They discuss freedom and the music born from the Atlantic slave trade.
583.q: Well, freedom is what this whole thing is about, and how this whole thing started. Because not having freedom, and what this music was born from... I hesitate to say, because everyone knows, but I also need to say, because you think of what atrocities this music came out of, you have an entire...…

80.t: His theory of how jazz began, and clapping on the wrong beat
80.s: He thinks jazz came out of communal singing and gospel feeling that cannot be taught, and objects to a TV singer clapping the wrong beat.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: Another reason I'm glad you asked me that. Let me mention this. To my mind -- I've had a lot of people come up, I've heard them ask others, how was jazz started? Who started jazz? 145.t: Jazz as black heritage and invention out of frustration
145.s: Blues grew from despair and jazz from being denied, inventing to outdo imitators.
145.q: : Quite so. There's quite a possibility of just that, because blues singing, as a whole, came from despair and things that were wrong in peoples' lives, where people were tearing their hearts out, and singing it and putting it into musical form and fashion. 65.t: Rumba names, composers and the dances behind them
65.s: He names guaguanco composers, explains yuca and malanga rumba names, and says Cuban numbers always came with a dance, unlike bossa nova.
65.q: Yes. 96.t: Jazz as the wedding of African rhythm and European harmony
96.s: He and Johnston agree jazz is African rhythm joined to European melody and harmony.
96.ch: Chicago boyhood and the Austin High Gang

75.s: Dance asks about Native American influence; Ramirez ties Jazz to church revival beat with hand-clapping accents.
